lessons.title: Propositions, connectives and truth tables
lessons.summary: Connectives combine true-or-false propositions; inclusive OR includes the case where both inputs hold.
lessons.body:
Every `if` statement you have written is a small piece of logic. Propositional logic is the precise version of that: a way of combining true/false statements and working out, mechanically, when the combination is true.

It is the foundation for everything else in this module. Proofs are built from it, predicate logic extends it, and the SAT problem in the last lesson asks one question about it that turns out to be enormously hard and enormously useful.

## Propositions

In the classical two-valued logic used here, a proposition is a statement that is either true or false, never both.

- "7 is prime" is a proposition (true).
- "2 plus 2 equals 5" is a proposition (false).
- "x is greater than 3" is **not** a proposition on its own: its truth depends on what the unknown x is. (Predicate logic, next lesson, handles this.)
- "Close the door" is not a proposition: it is neither true nor false.

We name propositions with letters: p, q, r. These are **propositional variables**, the logical equivalent of Boolean variables in code. When we write down the truth values themselves, T means true and F means false.


## The connectives

Five connectives build bigger formulas from smaller ones. Each has its own symbol, and these symbols appear in every lesson of this module, so it is worth learning them now.

```formula essential
¬p
p ∧ q
p ∨ q
p → q
p ↔ q
where
p, q: propositions (propositional variables), each either true or false
¬: NOT (negation). ¬p is true exactly when p is false
∧: AND (conjunction). p ∧ q is true only when both p and q are true
∨: OR (disjunction). p ∨ q is true when at least one of p, q is true, including when both are
→: IMPLIES (implication, the conditional). p → q reads "if p then q", and is false only when p is true and q is false
↔: IF AND ONLY IF (the biconditional). p ↔ q is true when p and q have the same truth value, both true or both false
In words: "not p", "p and q", "p or q", "if p then q" and "p if and only if q": the five ways to build a bigger statement out of p and q.
```

The table gives each one's name and the nearest Python.

| Symbol | Name | Read as | Python |
|---|---|---|---|
| not p | negation | not p | `not p` |
| p and q | conjunction | p and q | `p and q` |
| p or q | disjunction | p or q | `p or q` |
| p implies q | implication | if p then q | `(not p) or q` |
| p if and only if q | biconditional | p if and only if q | `p == q` |

The Python column assumes Boolean operands. Python and/or return operands and short-circuit; arbitrary objects can have custom truth tests and equality. The logical connectives have their meaning fixed by a **truth table**, which lists every combination of inputs, one per row. Each variable doubles the number of combinations, because every existing row splits into a "true" version and a "false" version:

With two Boolean inputs there are four possible assignments; with three there are eight. Adding an independent input doubles the work.

Here is the truth table for all five connectives over p and q. T is true and F is false; each column is one connective.

```
p q | ¬p  p∧q  p∨q  p→q  p↔q
----+-------------------------
T T |  F   T    T    T    T
T F |  F   F    T    F    F
F T |  T   F    T    T    F
F F |  T   F    F    T    T
```

Two things trip people up.

- **∨ is inclusive.** p or q is true when both are true. "Exclusive or" (exactly one) is a separate connective, written ⊕. In Python on booleans it is `p != q`.
- **→ is false in exactly one row**: when p is true and q is false.

Exclusive OR accepts the two cases where the inputs differ and rejects the two cases where they agree.


## Key takeaways
- Connectives combine true-or-false propositions; inclusive OR includes the case where both inputs hold.
- Every independent Boolean input doubles the number of rows of the truth table.

## Further reading
- [MIT Mathematics for Computer Science](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-042j-mathematics-for-computer-science-spring-2015/mit6_042js15_textbook.pdf)
- [Propositional calculus — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Propositional_calculus)

questions.prompt: A service adds one new independent Boolean feature flag. What happens to the number of test cases needed to check every combination of flag settings?

options.text: It increases by two
options.explanation: That would test the new flag separately, missing its combinations with existing settings.

options.text: It stays the same
options.explanation: Every existing combination can now occur with the new flag either off or on.

options.text: It doubles
options.explanation: Correct. Each old assignment splits into an off case and an on case for the new flag.

options.text: It depends only on the order of the flags
options.explanation: Reordering independent flags does not change their possible value combinations.

questions.workedExample: Keep each existing test assignment and run it twice: once with the new flag off and once with it on. Both settings are independent possibilities. The required coverage therefore doubles, which explains why exhaustive testing grows rapidly.

questions.prompt: Two Boolean health checks, p and q, should trigger an alert exactly when they disagree. Which conditions implement that rule? Select all that apply.

options.text: p has the same truth value as not q
options.explanation: Correct. Matching the negation means the original checks differ.

options.text: not p has the same truth value as not q
options.explanation: Negating both checks preserves agreement, so this alerts on agreement.

options.text: At least one check is true, but they are not both true
options.explanation: Correct. This accepts exactly the two disagreement cases.

options.text: If p then q, and if q then p
options.explanation: Together these implications require agreement, the opposite of the intended alert.

questions.workedExample: The alert should fire when exactly one input is true. Comparing one input with the negation of the other does that, as does requiring at least one input while excluding both. Negating both inputs preserves their agreement; requiring each to imply the other also tests agreement.

lessons.title: Reading implications and contrapositives
lessons.summary: An implication fails only when its premise holds and its conclusion fails.
lessons.body:
## Why implication works this way

The bottom two rows of p implies q surprise everyone. Why is "if p then q" true whenever p is false? Here is the rule in one place:

The condition is false only when the premise is true and the conclusion is false. A false premise cannot violate this particular rule.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A conditional dinner promise
> “If you pass the exam, I will buy you dinner.” Passing without receiving dinner breaks that promise; failing leaves the dinner decision open.
>
> **How it maps:** Passing is the premise and buying dinner is the conclusion. Only a true premise with a false conclusion violates the implication.
>
> **Where it stops:** Material implication records truth values, not intentions, causes or whether a promise is fair.

This is called **vacuous truth**, and it matters. "Every element of the empty list is negative" is true, because there is no element to break it. Python agrees: `all([])` is `True`.

The connective defined by this table is the **material conditional**. It says nothing about cause. "If 2 plus 2 equals 5 then the Moon is cheese" is true, because the premise is false. That feels wrong in English, but it is the definition that makes proofs work.

> [!tip] Reading p implies q
> All of these mean p implies q: "if p then q", "p implies q", "p only if q", "q if p", "p is sufficient for q", "q is necessary for p". The phrase "p only if q" catches people out: it means p cannot happen without q, which is p implies q, not q implies p.


## Converse, inverse, contrapositive

From an implication p implies q you can form three related statements by swapping the two sides, negating both, or doing both:

```formula essential
p → q
q → p
¬p → ¬q
¬q → ¬p
where
p → q: the original implication, "if p then q"
q → p: the converse: the two sides swapped
¬p → ¬q: the inverse: both sides negated
¬q → ¬p: the contrapositive: swapped and negated
p, q: propositions, each true or false
¬: NOT: ¬p is true exactly when p is false
→: implies: false only when the left side is true and the right side is false
In words: the original, its converse, its inverse and its contrapositive. Only the contrapositive always has the same truth table as the original.
```

| Name | Form | Same as p implies q? |
|---|---|---|
| Contrapositive | not q implies not p | Yes, always |
| Converse | q implies p | Not in general |
| Inverse | not p implies not q | Not in general |

"If it is raining, the ground is wet" does not mean "if the ground is wet, it is raining" (a sprinkler could be on). That is the converse, and assuming it is one of the most common reasoning errors in proofs, code reviews and incident postmortems.

The contrapositive, "if the ground is not wet, it is not raining", is equivalent. You can check by truth table: both are false in exactly one row: p true and q false. The converse and the inverse are equivalent to *each other* (one is the contrapositive of the other).


## Key takeaways
- An implication fails only when its premise holds and its conclusion fails.
- Only the contrapositive is always equivalent to the original implication; a converse needs separate justification.

## Further reading
- [MIT Mathematics for Computer Science](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-042j-mathematics-for-computer-science-spring-2015/mit6_042js15_textbook.pdf)
- [Truth table — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truth_table)

questions.prompt:
A function's docstring promises: "If the input list is sorted, the output list is sorted." You call it with an **unsorted** list and get an unsorted list back. Has the promise (read as p implies q) been broken?

*Symbols: → means "implies" (if ... then).*

options.text: Yes: the output is unsorted, so q is false and the implication is false
options.explanation: This ignores p. An implication is only false when p is true *and* q is false. Here p (input sorted) is false.

options.text: No: p is false, so p implies q is true whatever the output is
options.explanation: Correct. With a false premise the implication is vacuously true. The docstring made no promise about unsorted inputs.

options.text: It cannot be decided without knowing whether the function sorts
options.explanation: The truth value of p implies q depends only on the truth values of p and q, not on how the function works internally. Both are known here.

options.text: Yes: an implication requires that q is false whenever p is false
options.explanation: That describes the inverse not p implies not q, which is not equivalent to p implies q. Reading the inverse into a promise is a classic error.

questions.workedExample: The promise applies only to sorted inputs. This input is unsorted, so this call cannot violate that promise. To refute it, find a sorted input whose output is unsorted.

questions.prompt: Your team's rule is: "If a pull request is merged, then CI passed." Which statement is **logically equivalent** to this rule?

options.text: If CI passed, then the pull request is merged
options.explanation: That is the converse (q implies p). It is not equivalent: CI can pass on a PR nobody has merged yet.

options.text: If the pull request is not merged, then CI did not pass
options.explanation: That is the inverse (not p implies not q). It is equivalent to the converse, not to the original rule.

options.text: If CI did not pass, then the pull request is not merged
options.explanation: Correct. This is the contrapositive (not q implies not p), which is always equivalent to p implies q.

options.text: The pull request is merged and CI passed
options.explanation: That is p and q, a much stronger claim. The rule does not assert that any PR is actually merged.

questions.workedExample: A merged pull request with failed CI would violate the rule. Saying “if CI did not pass, the request is not merged” forbids exactly that case. Passing CI alone does not require a merge.

questions.prompt:
What does this print?

```python
xs = []
# Compare all-items and any-item tests.
print(all(x > 0 for x in xs),
      any(x > 0 for x in xs))
```

options.text: `False False`
options.explanation: This treats "all" as needing at least one witness. A universal claim over nothing is vacuously true.

options.text: `True True`
options.explanation: `any` needs at least one element that satisfies the condition. An empty list has none, so `any` is False.

options.text: `True False`
options.explanation: Correct. "Every element is positive" has no element to refute it, so it is vacuously true. "Some element is positive" has no witness, so it is false.

options.text: It raises an exception for an empty iterable
options.explanation: Unlike `max([])`, `all` and `any` are defined on empty iterables: they return their identity values True and False.

questions.workedExample: `all` looks for a counterexample and finds none in the empty list, so it returns `True`. `any` looks for a witness and finds none, so it returns `False`. The output is `True False`.

questions.prompt:
A policy says: "You may deploy on Friday **only if** you have an approved change ticket." With d equals "you deploy on Friday" and t equals "you have an approved ticket", which formula captures it?

*Symbols: ∧ means AND; → means "implies" (if ... then); ↔ means "if and only if".*

options.text: t implies d
options.explanation: This says having a ticket forces a deploy. "Only if" names a necessary condition, not a sufficient one; this is the common mix-up.

options.text: d implies t
options.explanation: Correct. "d only if t" means d cannot happen without t: whenever d holds, t holds.

options.text: d if and only if t
options.explanation: That would be "if and only if". The policy does not say a ticket obliges you to deploy.

options.text: d and t
options.explanation: That asserts you do deploy and do have a ticket. A policy is a conditional rule, not a statement that the deploy happens.

questions.workedExample: “Only if” names a necessary condition. A Friday deployment must have approval, but approval by itself does not require deployment. The prohibited case is deploying on Friday without an approved change.

lessons.title: Classifying and comparing formulas
lessons.summary: A tautology is true on every assignment; a contradiction is false on every assignment.
lessons.body:
## Tautologies, contradictions, satisfiable formulas

Tautology, contradiction and contingency form three disjoint classes. Satisfiability is a related property that overlaps them. The two simplest examples, "p or not p" and "p and not p":

A statement OR its negation is always true in classical two-valued logic. A statement AND its negation is always false.

- A **tautology** is true in every row. Example: p or not p.
- A **contradiction** is false in every row. Example: p and not p.
- A **contingent formula** is true in some rows and false in others.
- A formula is **satisfiable** if at least one row makes it true: both tautologies and contingent formulas qualify.

These are linked: a formula A is a tautology exactly when its negation not A is unsatisfiable. SAT solvers exploit this to check that something *always* holds: they search for a row where it fails, and "no such row" is a proof.


A single propositional input, considered as a formula on its own, is contingent: the row where the input is true satisfies it and the row where the input is false does not. This also makes it satisfiable. By contrast, a contradiction has no satisfying row at all. These labels answer different questions: “does any assignment work?” is an existence question, while “does every assignment work?” is a universal question. Checking the negation changes the latter into a search for a counterexample.

## Key takeaways
- A tautology is true on every assignment; a contradiction is false on every assignment.
- Satisfiable means at least one assignment works, so tautologies and contingent formulas both qualify.

## Further reading
- [MIT Mathematics for Computer Science](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-042j-mathematics-for-computer-science-spring-2015/mit6_042js15_textbook.pdf)
- [Material conditional — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Material_conditional)

questions.prompt:
Which of these formulas are **tautologies** (true in every row)? Select all that apply.

*Symbols: ¬ means NOT; ∧ means AND; ∨ means OR (inclusive); → means "implies" (if ... then).*

options.text: (p implies q) or (q implies p)
options.explanation: Correct. If q is true, p implies q is true. If q is false, q implies p is true. Either way one disjunct holds.

options.text: (p implies q) implies (q implies p)
options.explanation: Not a tautology. It assumes an implication gives you its converse. In the row p false, q true, p implies q is true but q implies p is false, so the whole formula is false.

options.text: ((p implies q) and p) implies q
options.explanation: Correct. This is modus ponens written as a formula: whenever both premises are true, q is true.

options.text: ((p implies q) and q) implies p
options.explanation: Not a tautology. This is affirming the consequent. Row p equals F, q equals T makes both premises true and the conclusion false.

options.text: (p and not p) implies q
options.explanation: Correct. The premise p and not p is false in every row, so the implication is vacuously true everywhere. From a contradiction, anything follows.

questions.workedExample: Try to make the whole statement false. A cannot fail: when one implication fails, the reverse one holds. C cannot have a true premise and false conclusion, because its premise already includes the required implication and its premise. E has an impossible premise. B and D both fail when p is false and q is true.

lessons.title: Simplifying conditions with logical laws
lessons.summary: De Morgan changes AND to OR or OR to AND while negating both parts.
lessons.body:
## Logical equivalence

Two formulas are **logically equivalent** if they have the same truth value in every row. Equivalence means agreement on every allowed assignment, not merely agreement in the examples tested.

These are the laws you use daily to simplify conditions. The following two laws can be checked with a four-row truth table.

```formula essential
¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q
¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q
where
p, q: propositions, each true or false
¬: NOT: flips true and false
∧: AND: true only when both sides are true
∨: OR (inclusive): true when at least one side is true
≡: is logically equivalent to: same truth value in every row
In words: negating “both” means at least one part fails; negating “either” means both parts fail.
```

**De Morgan's laws** are the ones you will use most: to negate an AND, negate each part and switch to OR (and vice versa).

Commutativity means order doesn't matter; associativity means grouping doesn't matter. The identity laws say that AND with true and OR with false leave the other input unchanged. OR with true always succeeds; AND with false always fails.

> [!example] Simplifying a guard
> A code review finds `if not (user.banned or not user.verified):`. Assume Boolean attributes without side effects. Apply De Morgan and double negation.

Negate each alternative and join them with AND: the user must be not banned and not unverified. Double negation turns the latter into verified.

So it is `if not user.banned and user.verified:`. With ordinary Boolean attributes, both guards admit exactly the same cases.

Python evaluates `and` and `or` from left to right and may stop early. A logical rewrite that changes evaluation order can therefore be unsafe if an expression raises an exception or has side effects. Check an object is not `None` before reading its attributes.

The same reasoning explains the failing case of an implication. Its premise must hold and its conclusion must fail. That describes the same single failing row as the truth-table definition.


## Key takeaways
- De Morgan changes AND to OR or OR to AND while negating both parts.
- A derivation preserves truth only when every step applies a valid equivalence.

## Further reading
- [MIT Mathematics for Computer Science](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-042j-mathematics-for-computer-science-spring-2015/mit6_042js15_textbook.pdf)
- [De Morgan's laws — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Morgan%27s_laws)

questions.prompt:
Simplify this guard, where `a` and `b` are booleans:

```python
if not (a and not b):
    ...
```

options.text: `if not a and b:`
options.explanation: This negates each part but forgets to flip `and` to `or`. De Morgan's law changes the connective as well as negating the parts.

options.text: `if not a or not b:`
options.explanation: This flips `and` to `or` but fails to cancel the double negation on b: not not b is b, not not b.

options.text: `if a or b:`
options.explanation: This drops the negation on a altogether. Check a true, b false: the original is false, but `a or b` is true.

options.text: `if not a or b:`
options.explanation: Correct. By De Morgan and double negation, `not (a and not b)` becomes `not a or b`, which is also "if a then b".

questions.workedExample: The original guard rejects exactly the case where a is true and b is false. Its opposite wording is “a is false, or b is true”, which is `not a or b`. The other options either forget to change AND into OR or negate the wrong input.

questions.prompt:
This guard protects the happy path:

```python
if x is not None and x.size > 0:
    process(x)
```

You want an early-return guard for the opposite case. Which condition is **both** logically correct **and** safe to evaluate when `x` is `None`? Assume each non-None x has an ordinary integer size, with no side effects when reading it.

options.text: `if x is None or x.size <= 0: return`
options.explanation: Correct. De Morgan gives not a or not b, and short-circuit `or` stops after `x is None` is True, so `x.size` is never touched on None.

options.text: `if x.size <= 0 or x is None: return`
options.explanation: Logically equivalent ( or is commutative), but Python evaluates left to right, so `x.size` raises AttributeError when x is None. Logic ignores left-to-right execution; code does not.

options.text: `if x is None and x.size <= 0: return`
options.explanation: De Morgan applied without flipping `and` to `or`. It is wrong logically, and it crashes: when x is None it evaluates `x.size`.

options.text: `if x is not None or x.size <= 0: return`
options.explanation: Only the connective was flipped, not the first operand. It returns early for every non-None x, the opposite of what you want.

questions.workedExample: The early return must handle either a missing object or a nonpositive size. Check `x is None` first: a true result short-circuits OR and avoids accessing `x.size`. On a non-None object, the integer size comparison safely decides the other case.

lessons.title: Checking finite truth tables in code
lessons.summary: An exhaustive truth table proves an equivalence over its specified Boolean inputs.
lessons.body:
## Checking equivalence in code

With n variables there are only 2 to the power n rows, so a computer can check any equivalence by brute force.

```python
from itertools import product

def equivalent(f, g, n):
    # Visit every Boolean assignment.
    for v in product([False, True],
                     repeat=n):
        # Unpack inputs; stop at a mismatch.
        if f(*v) != g(*v):
            return False, v
    # All rows matched: no counterexample.
    return True, None

imp = lambda p, q: (not p) or q
contra = lambda p, q: imp(not q, not p)
conv = lambda p, q: imp(q, p)

# Same truth values for all four pairs.
print(equivalent(imp, contra, 2))
# A false premise separates the converse.
print(equivalent(imp, conv, 2))
```

The output is `(True, None)` then `(False, (False, True))`. The second line hands you a counterexample: with p false and q true, p implies q is true but its converse q implies p is false.

How far does brute force go? Count the rows:

Twenty inputs already need about a million rows. Every additional input doubles that work; sixty need over a billion billion rows.

This is often practical for small numbers of Boolean inputs. Exhaustive work at sixty variables is far larger; the actual runtime depends on the cost of evaluating each row. That gap is the subject of the SAT lesson.


## Precedence

By convention, ¬ binds tightest, then ∧, then ∨, then →, then ↔. Implication is usually read right-associatively (grouped from the right):

```formula essential
¬p ∧ q → r   means   ((¬p) ∧ q) → r
p → q → r    means   p → (q → r)
where
p, q, r: propositions, each true or false
¬: NOT: applies only to the thing directly after it
∧: AND: binds more tightly than → (it is grouped first)
→: implies: binds more loosely than ¬ and ∧
In words: NOT is applied first, then AND, then OR, then implication; a chain of implications groups from the right.
```

Python follows the same order for `not`, `and`, `or`. When in doubt, add brackets: other people will read the code too.


## Key takeaways
- An exhaustive truth table proves an equivalence over its specified Boolean inputs.
- Exponential growth makes exhaustive enumeration impractical for many variables; explicit brackets clarify grouping.

## Further reading
- [MIT Mathematics for Computer Science](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-042j-mathematics-for-computer-science-spring-2015/mit6_042js15_textbook.pdf)
- [Functional completeness — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional_completeness)

questions.prompt: An exhaustive checker compares two Boolean expressions for all assignments of their two Boolean inputs. It reports no difference. What has it established?

options.text: Equivalence for those Boolean inputs
options.explanation: Correct. Every assignment in the specified finite Boolean domain was checked.

options.text: Equivalent behaviour for arbitrary Python objects
options.explanation: Python objects can implement custom equality and truth tests, so the Boolean result does not establish this.

options.text: Efficient exhaustive checking for any number of variables
options.explanation: Every added Boolean variable doubles the number of rows, so the same method scales exponentially.

questions.workedExample: There are four Boolean pairs. Comparing both results in each pair covers the entire specified domain, so no untested Boolean assignment remains. That is a finite exhaustive proof. It does not extend to different input semantics or imply an efficient algorithm for much larger domains.

lessons.title: Valid arguments and reasoning errors
lessons.summary: Validity rules out a true-premises, false-conclusion assignment.
lessons.body:
## Valid arguments

A **logical argument** has premises and a conclusion. It is **logically valid** if the conclusion is true in every row where all the premises are true. Equivalently:

A valid argument has no assignment that makes all its premises true and its conclusion false.

The standard valid forms, written with derives ("therefore"):

```formula essential
p → q, p ⊢ q
p → q, ¬q ⊢ ¬p
p → q, q → r ⊢ p → r
p ∨ q, ¬p ⊢ q
p ∨ q, p → r, q → r ⊢ r
where
p, q, r: propositions, each true or false
,: separates the premises
⊢: "therefore": the formula on the right follows validly from the premises on the left. (Strictly ⊢ means "can be derived by the rules of a proof system", and ∴ is the usual "therefore" sign; for classical propositional logic the soundness and completeness theorems make ⊢ coincide with "true in every row where the premises are true", which is written ⊨)
→: implies
¬: NOT
∨: OR (inclusive)
In words: line by line, modus ponens, modus tollens, hypothetical syllogism, disjunctive syllogism and proof by cases (disjunction elimination).
```

| Rule | Premises | Conclusion |
|---|---|---|
| Modus ponens | p implies q, p | q |
| Modus tollens | p implies q, not q | not p |
| Hypothetical syllogism | p implies q, q implies r | p implies r |
| Disjunctive syllogism | p or q, not p | q |
| Proof by cases | p or q, p implies r, q implies r | r |

And two famous invalid ones:

- **Affirming the consequent**: from p implies q and q, conclude p. Invalid (row p equals F, q equals T).
- **Denying the antecedent**: from p implies q and not p, conclude not q. Invalid (same row).

For both errors, let p be false and q true. The original implication holds. Affirming the consequent then wrongly concludes p; denying the antecedent wrongly concludes not q. Each argument has true premises and a false conclusion.

> [!warning] Debugging with the converse
> "If the cache is down, latency spikes. Latency spiked, so the cache is down." That is affirming the consequent. Latency spikes have many causes. Modus tollens is the safe direction: "latency did not spike, so the cache is not down" (given the premise holds).

Validity is about form, not truth. "If pigs fly, I am the Queen; pigs fly; so I am the Queen" is valid. Its conclusion is false only because a premise is false. An argument that is valid *and* has true premises is called a **sound argument**.


## Key takeaways
- Validity rules out a true-premises, false-conclusion assignment.
- Affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent are invalid even when a particular conclusion happens to be true.

## Further reading
- [MIT Mathematics for Computer Science](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-042j-mathematics-for-computer-science-spring-2015/mit6_042js15_textbook.pdf)
- [Mathematics for Computer Science — MIT OpenCourseWare](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-042j-mathematics-for-computer-science-spring-2015/)

questions.prompt: In an incident review someone argues: "If the new deploy is faulty, the error rate rises. The error rate rose. So the new deploy is faulty." What is the status of this argument?

options.text: Valid: it is modus ponens
options.explanation: Modus ponens goes from p implies q and **p** to q. Here we are given q and conclude p, which is the reverse.

options.text: Valid: it is modus tollens
options.explanation: Modus tollens goes from p implies q and not q to not p. Nothing here is negated.

options.text: Invalid: it affirms the consequent
options.explanation: Correct. From p implies q and q you cannot conclude p. The error rate could have risen for another reason, such as a downstream outage.

options.text: Valid, but only if the premise is true
options.explanation: Validity is about form, not about whether the premises happen to be true. This form is invalid even when every premise is true.

questions.workedExample: A downstream outage could raise the error rate while the deploy remains sound. Then both stated premises hold, yet the proposed conclusion is false. That counterexample shows the argument affirms the consequent.

questions.prompt:
Every request is served by region A or region B (p or q). If served by A it is logged (p implies r). If served by B it is logged (q implies r). Is the conclusion "the request is logged" (r) a **valid** consequence of these premises?

*Symbols: ∨ means OR (inclusive); → means "implies" (if ... then).*

options.text: No: we don't know which region served it, so we can't conclude r
options.explanation: You don't need to know which disjunct holds; both cases lead to r. This is reasoning by cases.

options.text: Yes: in every row where all three premises are true, r is true
options.explanation: Correct. This form (p or q, p implies r, q implies r derives r) is valid. It is the logic behind proof by cases.

options.text: Only if exactly one region serves each request
options.explanation: ∨ is inclusive and the argument works even if both p and q are true; r follows either way.

options.text: No: this is affirming the consequent
options.explanation: Affirming the consequent concludes p from p implies q and q. Here we conclude the consequent r, which is the safe direction.

questions.workedExample: At least one region served the request. If it was A, A's guarantee gives logging. If it was B, B's guarantee gives logging. Both cases reach the same conclusion, even if both regions served it.

lessons.title: Building every connective from NAND
lessons.summary: A functionally complete collection expresses every Boolean truth table.
lessons.body:
## How many connectives do you need?

Not five. Implication and the biconditional can be rewritten with the others, and OR can be rewritten with NOT and AND:

Implication can be expressed as NOT-premise OR conclusion. A biconditional combines implications in both directions. De Morgan then rewrites OR using only NOT and AND.

NOT, AND and OR can express every Boolean truth table: describe each accepted row with an AND of its required input values, then join the accepted rows with OR. De Morgan shows that NOT and AND alone suffice too. A set like this is **functionally complete**.

Remarkably, a single connective is enough: **NAND** ("not and"), written ↑. Feeding a value into both inputs of a NAND negates it, which is the key to building the rest:

```formula essential
p ↑ q ≡ ¬(p ∧ q)
¬p ≡ p ↑ p
p ∧ q ≡ (p ↑ q) ↑ (p ↑ q)
p ∨ q ≡ (p ↑ p) ↑ (q ↑ q)
where
p, q: propositions, each true or false
↑: NAND (not and): false only when both sides are true
¬: NOT
∧: AND
∨: OR
≡: is logically equivalent to
In words: NAND is "not both". NAND of a value with itself is its negation; NAND of a NAND gives AND back; NAND of two negations gives OR (by De Morgan).
```

Check the AND line with p equals T and q equals T: p NAND q is F, and F NAND F is T, which matches p and q.

This is why chips can be built from NAND gates alone. NOR is also complete on its own; AND, OR and NOT individually are not.


## Key takeaways
- A functionally complete collection expresses every Boolean truth table.
- NAND alone can express negation, AND and OR; neither AND nor OR alone suffices.

## Further reading
- [MIT Mathematics for Computer Science](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-042j-mathematics-for-computer-science-spring-2015/mit6_042js15_textbook.pdf)

questions.prompt:
You are building logic from NAND gates only, where p NAND q is equivalent to not (p and q). Which circuit computes p implies q?

*Symbols: ¬ means NOT; ∧ means AND; → means "implies" (if ... then); ≡ means "is logically equivalent to"; ↑ means NAND (not both).*

options.text: (p NAND p) NAND q
options.explanation: (p NAND p) is not p, so this is not (not p and q), which is p or not q, which is q implies p. That is the converse, not p implies q.

options.text: (p NAND q) NAND (p NAND q)
options.explanation: This NANDs a value with itself, which negates it: not not (p and q) is equivalent to p and q. It computes AND.

options.text: (p NAND p) NAND (q NAND q)
options.explanation: This is not (not p and not q), which by De Morgan is p or q. It computes OR.

options.text: p NAND (q NAND q)
options.explanation: Correct. (q NAND q) is not q, so this is not (p and not q), which is not p or q, which is p implies q.

questions.workedExample: An implication fails only with p true and q false. NAND fails only when both its inputs are true. Feed p into one input and the negation of q into the other. NANDing q with itself supplies that negation, giving `p NAND (q NAND q)`.

lessons.title: Predicates, domains and quantifiers
lessons.summary: The domain determines which values a quantified variable may take.
lessons.body:
Propositional logic cannot say "every user has an email address" without listing every user. It treats each statement as an indivisible true-or-false value, with no way to talk about *things* and their *properties*.

**Predicate logic** (also called first-order logic) adds exactly that: variables that range over objects, properties of those objects, and the words "for all" and "there exists". It is the language most mathematics is written in, and it is what you are really writing when you use `all()`, `any()` or SQL's `EXISTS`.

## Predicates and domains

A **predicate** is a statement with variables, which becomes a proposition once you plug in values.

- Even(x): "x is even".
- Admin(u): "user u is an admin".
- Less(x, y): "x is less than y", a predicate of two variables.

Plugging in a value gives a plain true-or-false proposition:

For example, “4 is even” is true, “7 is even” is false, and “2 is less than 5” is true. Supplying values turns each predicate into a proposition.

Every variable ranges over a **domain** (or **universe of discourse**): the set of things it may stand for. The domain is part of the meaning. "There is a number whose square is 2" is true over the real numbers (the square root of 2, about 1.414) and false over the integers.


## The two quantifiers

Two symbols turn a predicate into a proposition about the whole domain:

```formula essential
∀x P(x)
∃x P(x)
where
x: a variable ranging over the domain D
D: the domain, the set of things x may stand for
P(x): a predicate: a statement about x that is true or false once x is fixed
∀: "for all", the universal quantifier. ∀x P(x) is true when P(x) is true for every x in D
∃: "there exists", the existential quantifier. ∃x P(x) is true when P(x) is true for at least one x in D
In words: "P holds for every x" and "P holds for at least one x". The symbols are an upside-down A (for "All") and a backwards E (for "Exists").
```

| Symbol | Name | Meaning | Python |
|---|---|---|---|
| for every x P(x) | universal | P holds for every x | `all(P(x) for x in D)` |
| there exists x P(x) | existential | P holds for at least one x | `any(P(x) for x in D)` |

The Python analogy assumes finite iterables, terminating predicates and no side effects. On a finite domain {d₁, d₂, d₃}, the quantifiers are just big connectives:

On a finite domain, “for all” combines the results with AND, while “there exists” combines them with OR.

Standard first-order structures usually require a nonempty universe. Restricted quantification over an empty subset is still meaningful; the same conventions apply if empty universes are explicitly allowed. That explains the empty-set behaviour. An empty AND is true and an empty OR is false, so over an empty domain every ∀ statement is (vacuously) true and every ∃ statement is false. `all([])` is `True` and `any([])` is `False` for exactly this reason.

To **disprove** a ∀ claim you need one **counterexample**. To **prove** an ∃ claim you need one **witness**. Proving a ∀ claim over an infinite domain, or disproving an ∃ claim, needs an actual argument; that is what the next lessons are about.


## Key takeaways
- The domain determines which values a quantified variable may take.
- A universal claim needs all domain members; an existential claim needs one witness.

## Further reading
- [Open Logic Project](https://forallx.openlogicproject.org/)
- [First-order logic — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-order_logic)

questions.prompt: A program produces a prime number for each of forty tested inputs. An allowed input then produces 1681, which is 41 times 41. What does this establish about the claim “every allowed input produces a prime”?

options.text: The claim holds because most tests passed
options.explanation: A universal claim cannot tolerate even one counterexample.

options.text: The claim is still undecided until every input is tested
options.explanation: One counterexample already disproves it.

options.text: The earlier passing tests must be wrong
options.explanation: They may be correct; a claim can hold in those cases and fail elsewhere.

options.text: The claim is false
options.explanation: Correct. The supplied factorisation shows the output is composite for an allowed input.

questions.workedExample: The claim covers every allowed input. One allowed input with a composite output makes that universal claim false. The many successful tests remain valid observations, but cannot cancel the counterexample.

questions.prompt:
Consider this statement:

```formula essential
∀x ∃y (x · y = 1)
where
x, y: variables ranging over the chosen domain
·: multiplied by
∀: for all
∃: there exists at least one
In words: every x has some y in the domain that multiplies with it to give 1.
```

Over which domain is it **true**?

*Symbols: ∀ means "for all"; ∃ means "there exists at least one".*

options.text: The integers
options.explanation: For x equals 2 there is no integer y with 2y equals 1. Only x equals 1 and x equals −1 have integer inverses.

options.text: The real numbers
options.explanation: x equals 0 is a counterexample: 0 times y equals 0 for every y. A single counterexample sinks a ∀.

options.text: The positive real numbers
options.explanation: Correct. For any x is greater than 0, y equals 1/x is a positive real with x times y equals 1.

options.text: The natural numbers {0, 1, 2, ...}
options.explanation: Fails for both x equals 0 and x equals 2. Natural numbers are not closed under taking reciprocals.

questions.workedExample: The partner must exist inside the chosen domain. Zero has no reciprocal, so including zero defeats the claim. Integers also fail because two needs a fractional reciprocal. Every positive real has a positive real reciprocal, so that domain works.

lessons.title: Translating every and some correctly
lessons.summary: Restricted universal claims use an implication so non-members do not violate the rule.
lessons.body:
## Translating English

Most real statements quantify over *some* of the domain: "every admin", "some order". These **restricted quantifiers** have a fixed shape, and getting it wrong is the most common error in the whole subject. Over a domain of users:

```formula essential
∀u (Admin(u) → Verified(u))
∃u (Admin(u) ∧ Verified(u))
where
u: a variable ranging over all users
Admin(u): the predicate "u is an admin"
Verified(u): the predicate "u is verified"
∀: for all users
∃: there exists at least one user
→: implies: "if ... then ...", false only when the left side is true and the right side false
∧: AND: true only when both sides are true
In words: "every user, if an admin, is verified" (every admin is verified) and "some user is both an admin and verified" (some admin is verified).
```

The four common patterns (not is NOT):

| English | Formula |
|---|---|
| Every admin is verified | for every u (Admin(u) implies Verified(u)) |
| Some admin is verified | there exists u (Admin(u) and Verified(u)) |
| No admin is verified | for every u (Admin(u) implies not Verified(u)) |
| Not every admin is verified | there exists u (Admin(u) and not Verified(u)) |

For these restricted-domain translations, use implication under ∀ and conjunction under ∃. This is not a restriction on which connectives may appear in quantified formulas.

> [!warning] The two classic mistranslations
> - for every u (Admin(u) and Verified(u)) says *everyone* is an admin and verified. Far too strong.
> - there exists u (Admin(u) implies Verified(u)) is true as soon as there is a single non-admin, because the implication is then vacuously true. Far too weak.

In code the same shapes appear naturally. These are expressions to use with a finite iterable `users`; each account object must have Boolean `admin` and `verified` attributes. They produce Boolean results and do not print them:

```python
# Filtering ignores non-admin accounts.
all(u.verified for u in users
    if u.admin)

# One verified admin supplies a witness.
any(u.admin and u.verified
    for u in users)
```

The `if` filter in a comprehension plays the role of the →.


## Key takeaways
- Restricted universal claims use an implication so non-members do not violate the rule.
- Restricted existential claims require membership and the desired property together.

## Further reading
- [Open Logic Project](https://forallx.openlogicproject.org/)
- [Quantifier (logic) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantifier_(logic))

questions.prompt:
Over the domain of all user accounts, A(u) means "u is an admin" and T(u) means "u has two-factor auth enabled". Which formula says **every admin has two-factor auth**?

*Symbols: ∧ means AND; → means "implies" (if ... then); ∀ means "for all"; ∃ means "there exists at least one".*

options.text: for every u (A(u) and T(u))
options.explanation: This says every account is an admin *and* has 2FA. Using ∧ with ∀ makes the claim about the whole domain, not just admins.

options.text: for every u (A(u) implies T(u))
options.explanation: Correct. ∀ pairs with →: for each account, if it is an admin then it has 2FA. Non-admins satisfy the implication vacuously.

options.text: there exists u (A(u) and T(u))
options.explanation: This requires at least one 2FA-enabled admin. The universal rule requires every admin to be 2FA-enabled and is vacuously true if no admins exist; the two statements differ.

options.text: for every u (T(u) implies A(u))
options.explanation: This is the converse: every account with 2FA is an admin. It says nothing about admins without 2FA.

questions.workedExample: Test the rule on a regular account without 2FA. A rule about admins must allow that account. An implication does, because its admin premise is false. Conjunction would wrongly require that account to be an admin as well.

questions.prompt:
A compliance check is specified as there exists u (Admin(u) implies Verified(u)). It passes on a database with 1,000 **unverified** admins and one regular user. Why?

*Symbols: → means "implies" (if ... then); ∀ means "for all"; ∃ means "there exists at least one".*

options.text: The check is correct; at least one admin must be verified
options.explanation: No admin is verified here, so if it meant that, it should fail. The formula does not say what was intended.

options.text: Existential claims are always true over non-empty domains
options.explanation: there exists x P(x) is false whenever no element satisfies P. The issue is specifically the → inside ∃.

options.text: The regular user makes Admin(u) implies Verified(u) vacuously true, which is all ∃ needs
options.explanation: Correct. For the regular user, Admin(u) is false, so the implication is true and serves as a witness. ∃ should pair with ∧.

options.text: The database has more than one user, so ∃ becomes ∀
options.explanation: Quantifiers don't change with domain size. The check passed because of the shape of the formula, not the number of users.

questions.workedExample: An existential check needs one witness. The regular user's admin predicate is false, so its implication is true regardless of verification. To require a verified admin, the witness must satisfy both properties together.

lessons.title: Negating quantified requirements
lessons.summary: Negation swaps universal and existential quantifiers and negates the condition.
lessons.body:
## Negating quantifiers

Negation swaps the quantifier and pushes the ¬ inside. These are De Morgan's laws for quantifiers.

```formula essential
¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x)
¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x)
where
x: a variable ranging over the domain
P(x): a predicate, true or false for each x
¬: NOT: negates whatever follows it
∀: for all
∃: there exists at least one
≡: is logically equivalent to
In words: "not everything has P" means "something lacks P", and "nothing has P" means "everything lacks P".
```

"Not every test passed" means "some test did not pass"; skipped or pending tests are not automatically failed tests. "No test failed" means "every test did not fail".

With a restricted quantifier, the counterexample must belong to the restricted group:

To refute “every admin is verified”, find an actual admin who is unverified. A non-admin cannot be that counterexample.

> [!example] An SLO, negated
> Hypothetical universal requirement: "every completed request to /checkout takes at most 300 ms". Only completed requests count, and the boundary is inclusive.

The requirement fails if some completed checkout request takes more than 300 milliseconds. Exactly 300 milliseconds is permitted; the failing case is strictly greater.

One slow completed request refutes this universal requirement. Real SLOs commonly allow an error budget; this is not a recommendation to page on every slow request. Note that ≤ flips to >, not to <.


## Key takeaways
- Negation swaps universal and existential quantifiers and negates the condition.
- One offending completed request refutes a universal maximum request duration; a real service objective may allow an error budget.

## Further reading
- [Open Logic Project](https://forallx.openlogicproject.org/)
- [Classical Logic — Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-classical/)

questions.prompt:
A CI dashboard shows "Not all tests passed". Writing P(t) for "test t passed", which statement is equivalent? Assume all tests have completed and each result is pass or fail.

*Symbols: ¬ means NOT; ∀ means "for all"; ∃ means "there exists at least one".*

options.text: for every t not P(t): every test failed
options.explanation: This pushes the ¬ inside without flipping the quantifier. "Not all passed" is consistent with 99 of 100 passing.

options.text: not there exists t P(t): no test passed
options.explanation: This is equivalent to "every test failed", the same over-strong reading as the first option.

options.text: there exists t not P(t): at least one test failed
options.explanation: Correct. not for every t P(t) is equivalent to there exists t not P(t). One failing test is enough to make "all passed" false.

options.text: there exists t P(t): at least one test passed
options.explanation: This doesn't negate anything; it is compatible with every test passing, which the dashboard rules out.

questions.workedExample: With completed pass-or-fail results, the absence of universal success means at least one failure. It does not mean every test failed, and it does not establish that any passed.

questions.prompt:
Which of these are correct negations of for every x (A(x) implies B(x))? Select all that apply.

*Symbols: ¬ means NOT; ∧ means AND; ∨ means OR (inclusive); → means "implies" (if ... then); ∀ means "for all"; ∃ means "there exists at least one".*

options.text: there exists x (A(x) and not B(x))
options.explanation: Correct. Flip ∀ to ∃ and negate the inside: "not (if A then B)" is "A and not B".

options.text: for every x (A(x) implies not B(x))
options.explanation: This says no A is a B. It is not equivalent to the negation: with no A objects it is vacuously true, while not-every-A-is-B is false. If A objects exist, it requires all of them to fail B rather than just one.

options.text: there exists x not (not A(x) or B(x))
options.explanation: Correct. "If A then B" is the same as "not A or B", so this is "there is an x where (if A then B) fails", the negation. It simplifies to the first option.

options.text: there exists x (A(x) implies not B(x))
options.explanation: This negates only the consequent. It is true whenever some x is not an A (vacuous truth), so it is not the negation.

questions.workedExample: A counterexample must satisfy A and fail B. Option A states that directly. Option C says the implication is false for some object, which is the same condition. Requiring every A to fail B is stronger; allowing a non-A as a witness is too weak.

lessons.title: Quantifier order and witness choice
lessons.summary: A witness chosen after another variable may depend on that variable.
lessons.body:
## Nested quantifiers

Statements with several variables need several quantifiers, and their **order matters** when they are of different kinds.

Let the domain be people and L(x, y) mean "x trusts y".

- for every x there exists y L(x, y): everyone trusts somebody (possibly different people).
- there exists y for every x L(x, y): there is one person whom everyone trusts.

The second is much stronger. It implies the first, but not the other way round:

```formula essential
∃y ∀x L(x, y)  ⊨  ∀x ∃y L(x, y)
∀x ∃y L(x, y)  ⊭  ∃y ∀x L(x, y)
where
x, y: variables ranging over people
L(x, y): the predicate "x trusts y"
∀: for all
∃: there exists at least one
⊨: logically implies: in every domain and interpretation where the left side is true, the right side is true too
⊭: does not logically imply: some interpretation makes the left side true and the right side false
In words: if one person is trusted by everyone, then everyone trusts somebody. But everyone trusting somebody does not mean there is one person trusted by all.
```

A simple counterexample uses integers instead of people:

Every integer has a greater integer: choose its successor. There is no single integer greater than every integer, because that chosen integer itself has a successor.

Quantifiers of the **same** kind commute (can swap places):

Two universal quantifiers can swap order, as can two existential quantifiers. In each case the same pairs are covered. Mixed quantifiers need separate justification.

Nested quantifiers are nested loops:

```python
xs = [3, 1, 2]

# Each item needs a larger list member.
print(all(any(y > x for y in xs)
          for x in xs))     # False

# One member must dominate the whole list.
print(any(all(y >= x for x in xs)
          for y in xs))     # True
```

The first fails at x equals 3, since nothing in the list exceeds it. The second succeeds with the witness y equals 3.

To negate a nested statement, change each quantifier and negate the property:

Negating “everyone trusts someone” gives “someone trusts nobody”. Each quantifier changes kind, and the final trust condition is negated.


## Key takeaways
- A witness chosen after another variable may depend on that variable.
- A single witness that works for everyone is stronger than a potentially different witness for each person.

## Further reading
- [Open Logic Project](https://forallx.openlogicproject.org/)
- [The Open Logic Project (free textbooks)](https://builds.openlogicproject.org/)

questions.prompt:
Over services s and engineers e, let C(e, s) mean "e is on call for s". Your SRE lead says: "There is one engineer who is on call for every service." Which formula is that?

*Symbols: ∀ means "for all"; ∃ means "there exists at least one".*

options.text: for every s there exists e C(e, s)
options.explanation: This says every service has some on-call engineer, possibly a different one per service. It is the weaker statement.

options.text: there exists e for every s C(e, s)
options.explanation: Correct. One engineer e is chosen first, then the claim holds for every service with that same e.

options.text: for every e there exists s C(e, s)
options.explanation: This says every engineer is on call for at least one service, which is about engineers' workload, not coverage.

options.text: there exists s for every e C(e, s)
options.explanation: This says some service has every engineer on call for it. The roles of the variables are reversed.

questions.workedExample: Choose one engineer before considering the services. That same engineer must cover each service. Reversing the order would let each service choose a different engineer, so it would not establish shared coverage by one person.

questions.prompt:
What does this print?

```python
xs = [2, 4, 9]
ds = [2, 3]
# Each item may choose its own divisor.
a = all(any(x % d == 0 for d in ds)
        for x in xs)
# One divisor must work for every item.
b = any(all(x % d == 0 for x in xs)
        for d in ds)
print(a, b)
```

options.text: `True True`
options.explanation: This assumes for every x there exists d implies there exists d for every x. No single d divides all of 2, 4 and 9, so b is False.

options.text: `True False`
options.explanation: Correct. a is for every x there exists d (d divides x): 2 and 4 by 2, 9 by 3. b is there exists d for every x: neither 2 nor 3 divides every element.

options.text: `False False`
options.explanation: a only needs *some* divisor per x, and each element has one, so a is True.

options.text: `False True`
options.explanation: This is impossible on a non-empty list: there exists d for every x always implies for every x there exists d, so b True would force a True.

questions.workedExample: Two divides both two and four; three divides nine. Each item therefore has an allowed divisor, so `a` is true. Neither allowed divisor divides every item, so `b` is false. The output is `True False`; the distinction is whether the witness may change between items.

lessons.title: Reading Big-O as a quantified promise
lessons.summary: Big-O requires a fixed multiplier and threshold that work for all later input sizes.
lessons.body:
## A real definition: Big-O

Big-O describes an eventual upper bound on growth. For eventually nonnegative functions on natural-number inputs, choose one positive constant multiplier and one starting threshold. The scaled comparison function must then bound the cost at every input beyond that threshold. Both choices must stay fixed as the input grows.

```formula reference
f(n) = O(g(n))   iff
∃c > 0 ∃n_0 ∀n ≥ n_0 : f(n) ≤ c · g(n)
where
f(n): the function being bounded, e.g. an algorithm's step count for input size n
g(n): the bounding growth function, e.g. n or n^2
n: the input size, a natural number (0, 1, 2, …)
O(g(n)): "Big-O of g": grows no faster than a constant times g, once n is large enough
c: a positive constant multiplier, chosen by the prover
n_0: a non-negative integer threshold input size, chosen by the prover; the inequality only has to hold from n_0 upwards
∃: there exists at least one
∀: for all
≥, ≤: is at least, is at most
·: multiplied by
:: "such that" (separates the quantifiers from the condition)
>: greater than
In words: an asymptotic upper bound uses one fixed multiplier and one threshold that work for every later input size.
```

The order of the choices matters: you cannot increase the multiplier every time a larger input defeats it.

For a cost of three steps per item plus ten startup steps, four steps per item is an upper bound once the input has at least ten items. The multiplier and threshold remain fixed as the input grows.

Now consider what it takes to disprove the bound.

To disprove a proposed asymptotic bound, defeat every fixed multiplier and threshold: find a later input where the bound fails. One isolated small-input exception is insufficient.

For example, compare quadratic growth with linear growth:

A square grows faster than any fixed multiple of its input. Given any proposed multiplier and threshold, choose an integer beyond the threshold and larger than the multiplier. Its square then exceeds the proposed linear bound.

Negating the definition tells you exactly what you have to show.


## Key takeaways
- Big-O requires a fixed multiplier and threshold that work for all later input sizes.
- Disproving Big-O requires a violating input for every proposed multiplier and threshold.

## Further reading
- [Open Logic Project](https://forallx.openlogicproject.org/)
- [Mathematics for Computer Science — MIT OpenCourseWare](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-042j-mathematics-for-computer-science-spring-2015/)

questions.prompt: A Big-O upper bound promises that one fixed positive multiplier and one threshold make a nonnegative cost no greater than the scaled comparison function for every later integer input size. Which statement is exactly the negation of this promise, without demanding more than necessary?

options.text: One multiplier for which the cost eventually exceeds the bound
options.explanation: A larger multiplier might still work; refuting one candidate does not refute all candidates.

options.text: Every multiplier fails at every later input
options.explanation: This is stronger than necessary. One later violation per proposed multiplier and threshold is enough.

options.text: For every proposed multiplier and threshold, some input beyond that threshold violates the bound
options.explanation: Correct. This defeats every possible fixed bound.

options.text: One small input where the cost exceeds the unscaled comparison function
options.explanation: The definition permits a multiplier and ignores a finite initial range.

questions.workedExample: A Big-O claim promises one fixed multiplier and one threshold that work for every later input. To refute it, defeat every proposed pair by finding a later violating input. You need not show failure at every later input, and a single early exception is insufficient.

lessons.title: Quantifier laws and variable scope
lessons.summary: Universal quantification distributes over AND; existential quantification distributes over OR.
lessons.body:
## Quantifiers and connectives

Some laws let you split quantified statements; some look similar but only hold in one direction:

```formula essential
∀x (P(x) ∧ Q(x)) ≡ ∀x P(x) ∧ ∀x Q(x)
∃x (P(x) ∨ Q(x)) ≡ ∃x P(x) ∨ ∃x Q(x)
∀x P(x) ∨ ∀x Q(x) ⊨ ∀x (P(x) ∨ Q(x))
∃x (P(x) ∧ Q(x)) ⊨ ∃x P(x) ∧ ∃x Q(x)
where
x: a variable ranging over the domain
P(x), Q(x): predicates, true or false for each x
∀: for all
∃: there exists at least one
∧: AND
∨: OR
≡: is logically equivalent to (holds both ways)
⊨: logically implies (holds left to right only)
In words: "for all" splits over AND and "there exists" splits over OR, in both directions. "For all" over OR and "there exists" over AND only work one way.
```

Why not the reverse of the last two? Over the integers:

Every integer is even or odd, but integers do not all share the same parity. Likewise, separate even and odd witnesses do not produce a number that is both.

Similarly, there is an even number and there is an odd number, but no number is both, so the ∃-over-AND law can't be reversed either.


## Free and bound variables

In the formula below, x is a **bound variable**, while y is a **free variable**:

```formula essential
∀x (x > y)
∀x P(x) ≡ ∀z P(z)
where
x, z: bound variables: each belongs to the quantifier in front of it, like a loop variable
y: a free variable: nothing quantifies it, so its value must come from outside
P: any predicate
>: is greater than
∀: for all
≡: is logically equivalent to
In words: a free variable needs an externally supplied value. A bound variable belongs to its quantifier; renaming it consistently to a fresh name, without capturing any free variable, preserves meaning.
```

An open formula is evaluated using an assignment to its free variables. Its truth may depend on that assignment, though an open formula can be true or false for every assignment in a particular structure. For example, over the integers the first displayed formula is false for every integer assigned to the free variable; there is always an integer no greater than it.

A bound variable is like a loop variable or a function parameter. Renaming it consistently to a fresh name, without capturing a free variable, changes nothing. Reusing the same name in nested scopes is legal but confusing, exactly as shadowing is in code.


## Key takeaways
- Universal quantification distributes over AND; existential quantification distributes over OR.
- Independent witnesses cannot generally be merged, and renaming bound variables must avoid capture.

## Further reading
- [Open Logic Project](https://forallx.openlogicproject.org/)

A colleague reasons: "Every request yesterday was served from the cache or from the database. Therefore either every request was served from the cache, or every request was served from the database." Is this valid?

lessons.title: Universal SQL queries and automation limits
lessons.summary: Double NOT EXISTS expresses the absence of a counterexample to a universal query.
lessons.body:
## Quantifiers in SQL

SQL has existence tests through EXISTS and quantified comparisons through ALL. It has no standalone FOR ALL quantifier for arbitrary predicates, so universal queries use the negation law:

A universal claim can be checked by searching for a counterexample: it holds exactly when no counterexample exists.

"Customers who have ordered **every** product" becomes a double `NOT EXISTS`:

For each customer, look for a product with no matching order. Keep the customer only when that search finds nothing.

```sql
SELECT c.id FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM products p
  WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM orders o
    WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
      AND o.product_id = p.id));
```

This pattern is called **relational division**. Assume customer and product IDs are non-null keys and matching order IDs identify those keys. If the products table is empty, every customer is returned: vacuous truth again.

Ordinary SQL comparisons involving `NULL` produce UNKNOWN, and `WHERE` keeps only TRUE rows. Use `IS NULL` to test directly for the missing-value marker. `EXISTS` itself returns TRUE or FALSE according to whether its subquery returns any rows. De Morgan's laws still hold for SQL's three truth values; the difference from classical logic is that a condition and its negation can both be UNKNOWN.


## How far can you automate it?

For propositional logic, you can always decide whether a formula is valid by checking every row (slowly). First-order logic is different. Church and Turing proved in 1936 that no algorithm can decide validity for every first-order formula. Gödel's completeness theorem says every valid formula has a proof, so you can *search* for proofs, but the search may run forever on a formula that is not valid.

In practice, tools such as Z3 and the Dafny verifier handle large, useful parts of it automatically. The undecidability shows up as timeouts and "unknown" answers, especially around quantifiers.


## Key takeaways
- Double NOT EXISTS expresses the absence of a counterexample to a universal query.
- General first-order validity is undecidable even though valid formulas have finite proofs.

## Further reading
- [Open Logic Project](https://forallx.openlogicproject.org/)
- [PostgreSQL subquery expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-subquery.html)
- [PostgreSQL comparisons and NULL](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-comparison.html)
- [PostgreSQL logical operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-logical.html)

questions.prompt:
This query returns customers who ordered every product:

```sql
SELECT c.id FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
 SELECT 1 FROM products p
 WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders o
  WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
  AND o.product_id = p.id));
```

The `products` table is accidentally truncated to zero rows. What does the query return?

options.text: No rows, because no customer ordered any product
options.explanation: This reads ∀ as needing evidence. Over an empty set of products, "ordered every product" is vacuously true.

options.text: Every customer
options.explanation: Correct. The inner subquery over products has no rows, so `NOT EXISTS` is true for every customer: "for all products" over an empty domain is true.

options.text: Only customers with at least one order
options.explanation: Logically every customer qualifies regardless of orders. The database optimizer determines the physical execution plan; SQL semantics do not prescribe whether a table is scanned.

options.text: An error, because a correlated subquery over an empty table is invalid
options.explanation: SQL handles empty tables in subqueries normally: `EXISTS` over zero rows is simply false.
